newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac seen readying call for snap poll on Monday.
newsitem.headline: Chirac seen readying call for snap poll on Monday.

text.p: President Jacques Chirac's office stayed tight-lipped amid feverish speculation he was readying a call for a snap general election on Monday, with surveys showing most voters wanted an early poll and predicting a close-run battle.

Chirac's spokeswoman would only deny a report in Le Monde that he was planning a sharp swing towards free market economic policies. Newspapers including Le Monde reported Chirac would go on television on Monday to call a two-stage election on May 25-June 1 or June 1-8.

Le Monde said Prime Minister Alain Juppe would set out campaign policies on Tuesday including a new round of austerity -- speeding up tax cuts and limiting the role of the state -- to help France qualify for the European Union's single currency.
"The allegations contained in that article concerning a so-called instruction on a change in economic policy are completely baseless," Chirac's spokeswoman said.

Parties including those of Chirac's centre-right coalition made contingency plans and aides said Socialist Party leader Lionel Jospin, head of the biggest opposition force, may unveil campaign themes in a televised interview at seven p.m. (1700 GMT).

Deputy Jacques Baumel, a senior member of Chirac's Gaullist RPR party, said the head of state was tempted by a snap election "because we need a strong message to the nation and a government reshuffle would not be sufficient.
"We must spare ourselves nine months of campaigning. There are vital economic decisions on Europe due soon and it is important the French be consulted," he told France-2 television.

Socialist spokesman Francois Hollande said a snap poll would amount to an admission that the government had reached an impasse -- "political, economic, because unemployment is increasing, and fiscal, because deficits are widening.
"Chirac knows failure is due in 1998 and he is making a bet he can beat the opposition now," Hollande said.

Chirac's silence has fanned press speculation that he may try to renew his majority and clear the decks for a crucial year in European integration. The National Assembly's five-year term expires in March 1998.
The presidency itself would not be affected by a snap poll. Chirac was elected in 1995 and has another five years to serve.

Most voters are dissatisfied with both Chirac and Juppe and 59 percent (against 38 percent) would welcome an early general election, according to an IFOP opinion poll published on Sunday by the weekly Journal du Dimanche.
The poll said 56 percent gave Chirac the thumbs-down (against 55 percent a month ago) and 31 percent approved of him (against 32 percent in March).
Juppe was credited with 61 percent of negative opinions (against 60 percent in March) and 27 percent of favourable opinions (against 29 percent).
Recent opinion polls have predicted a close battle but differed on whether the centre-right or the left would win.

Juppe refused to confirm a snap election was due but told France-3 television: "The nature of a politician is that he must always be ready. I see much agitation. So people should calm down a little. This decision is entirely up to the president."
He added that he had long made clear his plan to stand in Bordeaux where he is mayor.

If he called a vote, Chirac was expected to argue that it was needed to prepare for Europe. The EU is due to decide early in 1998 which countries meet the criteria to join the single currency due to be launched in 1999.
Arthuis has denied reports that the government was facing problems in meeting Maastricht treaty budget criteria and so might be forced to introduce unpopular spending cuts.

Jean Boissonnat, ex-member of the Bank of France's monetary policy council, said snap elections would have two advantages -- cut the length of the campaign and facilitate the launch of tighter and unpopular austerity policies.
